claims.claim: Kleander documents Kay's admitted 'telescoping' (iconoclasm moved centuries earlier; a 750-year Reconquista compressed to one lifetime) so that historical loss lands on the same set of characters and intensifies emotional response.
claims.source: Anya Kleander, 'Present Reality in Historical Fantasy' (Honours dissertation, University of Stirling, 2008)
claims.quote: intensify the emotional and intellectual response to what really happened

claims.claim: Kleander quotes Kay's stated method of a quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity that reaches readers subliminally and builds trust.
claims.source: Anya Kleander, 'Present Reality in Historical Fantasy' (Honours dissertation, University of Stirling, 2008)
claims.quote: quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity

claims.claim: Kleander observes that Kay plants hints to Valentin's identity as Rhun throughout Tigana which only make sense in retrospect.
claims.source: Anya Kleander, 'Present Reality in Historical Fantasy' (Honours dissertation, University of Stirling, 2008)
claims.quote: the hints only make sense in retrospect

claims.claim: Kleander notes that who survived the Ammar–Rodrigo duel is not revealed until halfway through the epilogue, by which point the outcome is 'strangely unimportant'.
claims.source: Anya Kleander, 'Present Reality in Historical Fantasy' (Honours dissertation, University of Stirling, 2008)
claims.quote: not until halfway through the epilogue that Kay reveals who survived

claims.claim: Kleander sets side by side two near-identical prayer paragraphs (Asharite and Jaddite) as the clearest example of Kay using structural repetition to show how alike the religions are.
claims.source: Anya Kleander, 'Present Reality in Historical Fantasy' (Honours dissertation, University of Stirling, 2008)
claims.quote: the clearest example of how alike the religions are

claims.claim: Kleander reads Pertennius (Procopius) as Kay's illustration that history is carved and chosen, with the narrator's opening line that writers of history seek the dramatic over the truth.
claims.source: Anya Kleander, 'Present Reality in Historical Fantasy' (Honours dissertation, University of Stirling, 2008)

claims.claim: Kleander (via Toolan) argues Kay's structure leaves the reader torn between different views rather than resolved.
claims.source: Anya Kleander, 'Present Reality in Historical Fantasy' (Honours dissertation, University of Stirling, 2008)

claims.claim: Rettino reads Tigana's first sentence ('In the autumn season of wine, word went forth...') as an entry in a chronicle lending historical flavour, then subverted when the reported death proves faked.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: reads like an entry in a chronicle

claims.claim: Rettino notes the narrator adopts a cautious, guessing persona ('perhaps because...') whose judgments the naive reader must nonetheless accept, the club-story authority of portal-quest fantasy.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: The narrator’s speculative persona supposedly only guesses

claims.claim: Rettino cites the Lions passage 'One hundred and thirty-nine citizens of Fezana... This was the way of it' as the omniscient historian's voice breaking the immersive character perspective.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)

claims.claim: Rettino shows the narrator's voice and Jehane's thoughts intersecting so that distanced background exposition is disguised as the character's reflections.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)

claims.claim: Rettino notes Jehane's noticing what is unusual, in free indirect discourse, dispenses world information without a guide figure.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: she notes, in free indirect discourse

claims.claim: Rettino argues that riselka prophecies foreshadow and expose the structural lines of Tigana, seams a mimetic novelist would hide.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: foreshadow and expose the structural lines in his novel

claims.claim: Rettino documents that Under Heaven's narrator speaks in several scenes in the voice of a later-dynasty historian, citing chroniclers' consensus and then departing from it with knowing irony.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: speaks in several scenes in the voice of a historian

claims.claim: Rettino points to the narrator's exclamation that Shen Tai 'hadn't even passed the examinations at that point!' as the moment author and historian-narrator blend.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)

verdicts.trueWording: telescoping … intensify … by bringing it home to the same set of characters
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200, browser UA). Page: iconoclasm 'came several hundred years after Justinian's reign'; Reconquista 'took place over a period of 750 years and not in the lifetime of any one man as Kay depicts it'; 'Such ‘telescoping of events’' (Kay, Rambles interview); Kay: 'telescoping events […] allows [him] to intensify the emotional and intellectual response to what really happened by bringing it home to the same set of characters'. Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: quiet, steady accumulation … almost subliminal way … trust in the author
verdicts.note: Page: 'Kay believes ‘that the quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity reach out to readers in an almost subliminal way’ and induces ‘trust in the author and the book’ (Kay in SFSite Interview 2000)'. Quote verbatim; subliminal reach and trust both present; it is Kay's stated belief quoted by Kleander.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay has hinted to Valentin’s identity throughout the book
verdicts.note: Page: 'Kay has hinted to Valentin’s identity throughout the book, though the hints only make sense in retrospect: Brandin once told Dianora that ‘there [were] precedents’ (T, 415) of marring ‘a whole and healthy man’ to create the king’s fool.' The Rhun limb is supported elsewhere on the same page: 'he focalizes through Rhun, Brandin’s Fool who is revealed to be Valentin, Prince of Tigana and Alessan’s father.' Quote verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: reveals who survived the battle of the ‘lions’ … strangely unimportant
verdicts.note: Page: 'It is not until halfway through the epilogue that Kay reveals who survived the battle of the ‘lions’, but by then the outcome is strangely unimportant.' The immediately preceding sentences establish the combat as Ammar vs Rodrigo ('When Ammar and Rodrigo meet in combat … a fight to the death between two men who love each other'). Quote verbatim; 'strangely unimportant' verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: clearest example … can be seen in the prayers of the Asharites and the Jaddites
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. The page then prints the two prayer paragraphs consecutively (LoAR 251-252 and the Jaddite counterpart), and they are near-identical in frame ('They prayed for strength and mercy, for purity of heart and mortal body, for the fulfilment of Ashar’s starlit visions / Jad’s bright visions … to Paradise'). Kleander frames it as 'Rather than focusing on differences, Kay focuses on similarities.' She demonstrates the parallel rather than naming it 'structural repetition', but the mechanism is on the page verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: Pertennius sets out to ‘choose, sever and carve’ among events
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that 'writers of history seek the dramatic over the truth' is the narrator's opening line, and that Kleander attaches it to the Pertennius reading — the dissertation quotes 'seek the dramatic over the truth' (StS, 3) in a later, separate passage about Kay's own licence ('Being thus free to ‘seek the dramatic over the truth’ Kay teaches that there is no such thing as an ‘objective truth’'), never calls it an opening line or a narrator's line, and the word 'narrator' appears only twice on the page, both times about focalization theory
verdicts.note: Quote 'exquisitely phrased vituperation' is verbatim ('depicts Crispin reading Pertennius’ ‘exquisitely phrased vituperation’ (LoE, 154)'). Supported limbs: Pertennius is 'Kay’s most obvious illustration of how ‘history can become dangerous when the creative aspect of its construction is concealed or unknown’'; 'Pertennius is modelled on Procopius'; 'As Pertennius sets out to ‘choose, sever and carve’ (White 1973, 288) among events'. Searched raw text for 'opening line', 'first line', 'writers of history': zero hits.

verdicts.trueWording: juxtaposition of different ideological orientations … left them ‘torn between different views’
verdicts.note: Page: 'Kay has shown his readers ‘a juxtaposition of different ideological orientations’ and left them ‘torn between different views’ (Toolan 1988, 74). It does not matter who won because, either way, one of the three is gone.' Quote verbatim including the internal single quotes; Toolan attribution and the unresolved ('rather than resolved') limb both supported by the following sentences.

verdicts.trueWording: opening passage reads like an entry in a chronicle … subverted
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Page quotes Tigana's first sentence in full ('In the autumn season of wine, word went forth … had drawn the last bitter breath of his exile and age and died' (11)), then: 'The opening passage reads like an entry in a chronicle and lends the novel a historical flavour … However, the historical rhetoric is subverted when the reader eventually discovers that Sandre has faked his own death.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: reader must nonetheless agree … authority of the club-story teller
verdicts.note: Page: quotes 'perhaps because [of Sandre], and certainly because he tended to be cautious and circumspect in all his ways' (12), then 'The narrator’s speculative persona supposedly only guesses at the reasons for Alberico’s actions, but the reader must nonetheless agree with it … Readers must accept the narrator’s judgement because they are too new to the world to judge otherwise … it adopts the authority of the club-story teller, becoming unquestionable', within the section on portal-quest fantasy. Also 'Despite the narrator-historian’s apparent attempt to be circumspect and cautious'. Quote verbatim; all limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: due to the narrator’s omniscient historian’s voice … a breach in … immersion
verdicts.note: Page: 'However, due to the narrator’s omniscient historian’s voice, the novel is not a perfectly immersive fantasy. For example, the following passage reveals a breach in the subjective perspective necessary for immersion: “One hundred and thirty-nine citizens of Fezana assembled in the newest wing of the castle that afternoon … This was the way of it” (26).' Quote verbatim; the cited Lions passage and the immersion-breaking limb both exact.

verdicts.trueWording: narrator subtly offers information … disguising it as Jehane’s thoughts
verdicts.note: Page: 'the narrator’s voice and the thoughts of Kay’s viewpoint characters frequently intersect … written in a distanced fashion that signals a passage that is chiefly in the narrator’s voice: “The current governor of Fezana was a puppet of Almalik’s …” (14). The narrator subtly offers information to the reader, disguising it as Jehane’s thoughts.' Quote verbatim; intersecting voices, distanced background exposition, and the disguise all supported.

verdicts.trueWording: dispenses information … after she encounters the unusual … contrasts with … wise guides
verdicts.note: Page: 'Jehane’s viewpoint dispenses information to the reader after she encounters the unusual: she notes, in free indirect discourse, that “the noise level this morning was really quite extraordinary” (9) … a way of dispensing information to reader that contrasts with the method in the portal-quest fantasy, in which information is revealed by authorities, such books and wise guides.' Quote verbatim; the 'without a guide figure' limb is the page's explicit contrast.

verdicts.trueWording: riselka’s prophecies foreshadow and expose the structural lines in his novel
verdicts.note: Page: 'Whereas historical novelists usually attempt to hide underlying story structures, fantasy novels expose story like a shirt with the seams on the outside (Attebery) … Another seam is in prophecy, which Kay brings into his novel through the riselka … The riselka’s prophecies foreshadow and expose the structural lines in his novel.' Quote verbatim; the 'seams a mimetic novelist would hide' limb is supported by the hide/expose contrast and the section's opening ('Tigana differs from realist discourse').

verdicts.trueWording: voice of a historian describing … historians … of later Kitan dynasties
verdicts.note: Page (Under Heaven section): 'His narrator speaks in several scenes in the voice of a historian describing the discourses of the mandarin-class historians and philosophers of later Kitan dynasties who look back on the time of the main narrative.' The consensus-then-departure limb is supported later on the same page: chronicles 'it was subsequently agreed with a degree of consensus' (588), 'the narrator places value on the consensus, like a scholar', and 'the narrator’s departure from historical consensus becomes clear' via 'the narrator’s knowing irony'. Quote verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: exclamation point is telling … Kay’s role as author blends with that of the narrator
verdicts.note: Page: 'The narrator remarks that Shen Tai was unimportant to the narrative, since he “hadn’t even passed the examinations at that point!” (689) The exclamation point is telling. It reveals the narrator’s knowing irony … At this point, the narrator’s departure from historical consensus becomes clear and Kay’s role as author blends with that of the narrator.' Quote verbatim; the blend-of-author-and-historian-narrator limb exact.
